title: The exception that swallows the two-year rule
subtitle: Automatically unfair dismissal and remedies
objectives: Identify the categories of dismissal that are automatically unfair and require no minimum period of qualifying service, distinguishing them from the ordinary unfair dismissal regime's two-year threshold
Explain the order in which an employment tribunal considers remedies for unfair dismissal, and what the basic award and the compensatory award each compensate for
Apply the automatically unfair categories and the remedies framework to new fact patterns, including recognising when the statutory cap on the compensatory award does not apply

leadingAuthorities.role: Automatically unfair dismissal connected with pregnancy, maternity or other family leave; no qualifying period required
Automatically unfair dismissal for making a protected disclosure (whistleblowing); no qualifying period, and the compensatory award cap is disapplied
Automatically unfair dismissal for asserting a statutory right in good faith, whether or not the right actually existed

leadingAuthorities.citation: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992, s 152
leadingAuthorities.role: Automatically unfair dismissal for trade union membership or activities; no qualifying period, sitting alongside the ERA 1996 categories
The remedies framework: reinstatement and re-engagement orders, the basic award, and the (usually capped) compensatory award

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Most students can recite 'two years' service to claim unfair dismissal' without hesitation. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the headline rule — this lesson is about the fact patterns where it simply doesn't apply.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below is weighted towards scenario questions: expect facts to sort through, not definitions to recite.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take your time over the list of protected categories in Part 2 — the remedies material in Parts 4 and 5 assumes you can already spot which category is in play.

overview.hook: An employee starts a new job on a Monday. By Thursday she has reported a serious safety failure to her manager. By Friday she has been dismissed. On the ordinary unfair dismissal rules she has no claim at all — she hasn't worked anywhere near the two years the law usually demands. And yet she may have one of the strongest unfair dismissal claims an employment tribunal will see all year. This lesson is about why.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. The statutory cap on the compensatory award is uprated every April and is not quoted here as a fixed figure — what matters for this lesson is the structure of the cap, and the categories of dismissal from which it is removed entirely, not this year's number.

parts.heading: The exception that swallows the two-year rule
parts.voice: argumentative — states the general rule, then shows how much of it the exceptions actually eat
body: You already know the headline rule from ordinary unfair dismissal: under s 108 ERA 1996, an employee generally needs two years' continuous service before a tribunal will even hear an unfair dismissal claim. Employers rely on this constantly — dismiss someone in their first eighteen months, on almost any ground, and the ordinary unfair dismissal regime simply has no purchase.

But a defined, closed list of dismissal reasons switches the qualifying period off entirely. Dismiss an employee for one of these reasons — whatever their length of service, even if they started that morning — and the dismissal is automatically unfair. There is no need to show the employer acted unreasonably, no *Burchell* investigation to assess, no range of reasonable responses to weigh. If the tribunal finds the reason (or principal reason) for dismissal falls within the list, unfairness follows as a matter of law.

The policy logic is worth holding onto, because it explains why the list looks the way it does: each category protects an employee from being punished for doing something the law specifically wants employees to feel safe doing — reporting wrongdoing, taking family leave, joining a union, insisting on a legal entitlement. Strip away the qualifying period in these cases and you strip away the single biggest incentive an employer would otherwise have to sack a troublesome employee quietly, before the two years run out.

components.definition: A dismissal falling within a defined statutory category (e.g. whistleblowing, pregnancy/maternity, trade union membership, asserting a statutory right) that is unfair as a matter of law once the reason is established, with no minimum period of qualifying service and no assessment of the employer's reasonableness.

interaction.prompt: An employee is dismissed after three weeks' service for making a protected disclosure about safety failures. Can she bring an unfair dismissal claim?
options: Yes — whistleblowing dismissals require no minimum period of service
No — she needs two years' service first, like any other unfair dismissal claim
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Section 103A ERA 1996 is one of the categories that switches off the qualifying period entirely — length of service is irrelevant to whether the claim can be brought.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — the two-year rule is the default, but whistleblowing dismissals are one of a defined list of exceptions where no qualifying period applies at all. Keep that list in mind as you read on.

parts.heading: The protected categories, and where each one lives
parts.voice: structural — a reference part students will return to
body: The automatically unfair categories are scattered across two Acts, which trips students up more than the substance does. Most sit in ERA 1996 ss 99–104 — a run of provisions each targeting one protected reason. One important category — trade union membership or activities — sits instead in TULRCA 1992 s 152, a different statute entirely, because trade union protections were consolidated there rather than folded into the ERA.

Learn these as a checklist tied to a citation, not a vague sense of 'things employers can't sack you for'. An exam problem will give you facts, not statute numbers — you're expected to recognise which provision the facts engage.

Four categories recur most often in problem questions, and this lesson focuses on them, though the list is longer: pregnancy, maternity or other family leave (s 99); making a protected disclosure — whistleblowing (s 103A); trade union membership or activities (TULRCA s 152); and asserting a statutory right in good faith (s 104). Others exist — health and safety dismissals under s 100, for instance — and share the same no-qualifying-period structure, but aren't this lesson's focus.

components.label: The automatically unfair categories (core four)
points: Pregnancy, maternity or family leave — ERA 1996 s 99 — dismissal connected with pregnancy, childbirth, or taking maternity/paternity/adoption/parental leave
Whistleblowing — ERA 1996 s 103A — dismissal where the reason (or principal reason) is that the employee made a protected disclosure
Trade union membership or activities — TULRCA 1992 s 152 — dismissal for being, or proposing to become, a member, or for taking part in union activities
Asserting a statutory right — ERA 1996 s 104 — dismissal for bringing proceedings to enforce a statutory right, or alleging in good faith that the employer infringed one
All four: no minimum period of continuous service is required to claim

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that makes this dismissal automatically unfair, rather than something the ordinary unfair dismissal test would have to assess.
interaction.scenarioText: Aisha has worked for her employer for four months. She raises a written grievance asserting she has not been paid the National Minimum Wage, which is correct. Two days later, without any other explanation offered, she is dismissed.
tappableSpans: worked for her employer for four months
raises a written grievance asserting she has not been paid the National Minimum Wage
interaction.correctSpan: raises a written grievance asserting she has not been paid the National Minimum Wage
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the trigger. Asserting a statutory right in good faith — here, the right to the minimum wage — engages s 104 ERA 1996 regardless of her four months' service.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the protected act itself, not the timing around it. The four months' service is a red herring here — s 104 needs no qualifying period at all — and what matters is that Aisha asserted a genuine statutory right.

parts.heading: Reading the whistleblowing provision closely
parts.voice: statute-first — works from the text outward
body: Section 103A is the category examiners return to most, because it looks straightforward and rarely is. The provision itself is short, but it sits on top of the 'qualifying disclosure' machinery in s 43B (covered in full in this module's whistleblowing lesson) — for this lesson, take it as given that a qualifying, protected disclosure has been made, and focus on what s 103A itself requires once that's established.

The statute asks a single causal question: was the reason, or if more than one the principal reason, for the dismissal that the employee made a protected disclosure? Not 'was a disclosure made at some point before the dismissal' — the disclosure has to be the reason the employer actually dismissed for. An employer who genuinely dismisses for unrelated poor performance, coincidentally shortly after a disclosure, has not necessarily breached s 103A — though a tribunal will scrutinise the timing and the employer's explanation hard.

Section 103A also does something no other automatically unfair category on this list does on its own: by operation of s 124(1A), the usual statutory cap on the compensatory award does not apply to a s 103A dismissal at all. Part 5 comes back to why that matters.

components.text: An employee who is dismissed shall be regarded for the purposes of this Part as unfairly dismissed if the reason (or, if more than one, the principal reason) for the dismissal is that the employee made a protected disclosure.
elements: That disclosure was the reason, or the principal reason, for the dismissal

interaction.prompt: Under s 103A, what does the employer's dismissal reason have to be for the dismissal to be automatically unfair?
options: The protected disclosure must be the reason, or the principal reason, for the dismissal
Any protected disclosure made at any time before dismissal is sufficient, regardless of why the employer actually dismissed
The employee must show the disclosure was the sole reason with no other factor in play
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Section 103A asks a causal question — reason or principal reason — not a mere sequence-of-events question, and it doesn't demand the disclosure be the only factor, just the main one.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Re-read the statutory language: it asks what the reason, or principal reason, for dismissal actually was — not just whether a disclosure happened to precede the dismissal, and not that it must be the sole cause with nothing else present.

parts.heading: Remedies: what a tribunal actually orders, and in what order
body: Winning an automatically unfair dismissal claim answers only the liability question. The remedy stage follows a specific statutory sequence under ss 112–124 ERA 1996, and tribunals are required to work through it in order rather than jumping straight to compensation.

First, the tribunal must explain to the claimant what reinstatement and re-engagement orders are and ask whether the claimant wishes the tribunal to make one (s 112(2)). Reinstatement treats the employee as if never dismissed, in the same job; re-engagement puts them into a comparable or suitable job with a different employer or role. If the claimant wants one, the tribunal considers whether it's practicable to order — including whether the employer can show it's practicable, and (for reinstatement) whether the employee caused or contributed to the dismissal to any extent making it just to order it.

If no reinstatement or re-engagement order is made — because the claimant doesn't want one, or it isn't practicable — the tribunal moves to compensation, which has two separate components. The basic award (s 119) is calculated like a statutory redundancy payment: a formula based on age, gross weekly pay (capped) and complete years of service, and it compensates for the fact of dismissal itself, not for any specific financial loss. The compensatory award (s 123) is different in kind: it compensates the claimant's actual, tribunal-assessed financial loss flowing from the dismissal — lost earnings, lost benefits, and reasonable future loss — subject to the claimant's duty to mitigate.

components.label: The remedy sequence
points: Step 1 — the tribunal asks whether the claimant wants reinstatement or re-engagement (s 112(2))
Step 2 — if so, the tribunal assesses practicability, including any contribution by the employee
Step 3 — if no order is made, the tribunal turns to compensation
Step 4 — basic award: a redundancy-style formula (age × capped weekly pay × years of service), compensating the fact of dismissal
Step 5 — compensatory award: the tribunal's assessment of the claimant's actual financial loss, subject to mitigation and (usually) a statutory cap

interaction.prompt: Put these remedy steps in the order a tribunal follows.
items: Tribunal asks whether the claimant wants reinstatement or re-engagement
Tribunal assesses whether such an order is practicable
If no order is made, the tribunal turns to compensation
Tribunal calculates the basic award, then assesses the compensatory award
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the sequence set out in ss 112–124 — reinstatement and re-engagement are considered first, and compensation is the fallback, not the starting point.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Check the order again — a tribunal must ask about reinstatement and re-engagement, and assess practicability, before it ever turns to calculating the basic and compensatory awards.

parts.heading: The cap, and where it vanishes
parts.voice: Socratic — sets up the trap before resolving it
body: Here's the question worth pausing on: is the compensatory award always subject to a statutory maximum? Most students answer yes without hesitation, because the cap is genuinely the default position — s 124 sets a ceiling on the compensatory award, whichever is lower of a set statutory figure (uprated annually) or 52 weeks' gross pay.

But s 124(1A) removes that cap entirely for certain automatically unfair dismissals — most importantly, whistleblowing dismissals under s 103A, and dismissals connected with health and safety activities under s 100. For those categories, the compensatory award is assessed purely on the claimant's actual loss, with no statutory ceiling at all. This is precisely why whistleblowing claims can produce some of the largest unfair dismissal awards a tribunal makes.

The exam trap follows directly: a problem question that hands you a whistleblowing dismissal and then asks you to 'apply the statutory cap' is testing whether you notice the cap doesn't apply at all — not whether you can do the arithmetic.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often apply the statutory cap mechanically to every compensatory award calculation, including whistleblowing and health and safety dismissals.
components.whyItsWrong: Section 124(1A) expressly disapplies the cap for dismissals under s 103A (whistleblowing) and s 100 (health and safety). Applying the cap to those categories understates the claimant's true entitlement and misses the specific statutory carve-out the facts are usually there to test.

interaction.prompt: Priya is dismissed after fourteen months' service, the tribunal finding the principal reason was a protected disclosure she made about financial irregularities. Her assessed financial loss comfortably exceeds the usual statutory cap. Does the cap limit her compensatory award?
options: No — s 124(1A) disapplies the cap for s 103A whistleblowing dismissals, so she recovers her full assessed loss
Yes — the cap applies to every compensatory award regardless of the dismissal reason
No — because she has less than two years' service, no cap could ever have applied to her in the first place
interaction.explanation: The cap is disapplied specifically because this is a s 103A dismissal, not because of her length of service (which is irrelevant to the cap question). Priya recovers her full tribunal-assessed loss.

testPool.prompt: Name the minimum period of continuous service an employee needs before bringing a claim under one of the automatically unfair dismissal categories.
testPool.modelAnswer: None — the automatically unfair categories require no minimum period of qualifying service at all, unlike the ordinary unfair dismissal regime's two-year threshold.

testPool.prompt: Name the statutory provision that makes dismissal for trade union membership or activities automatically unfair, and identify which Act it sits in.
acceptableAnswers: s 152 Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992
testPool.modelAnswer: Section 152 of the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992 — note it sits outside the ERA 1996, unlike most of the other automatically unfair categories.

testPool.prompt: Does a claim under s 99 ERA 1996 (pregnancy/maternity-related dismissal) require the employee to have completed a minimum period of continuous service?
options: No — automatically unfair categories require no qualifying period
Yes — the usual two-year period still applies

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the automatically unfair dismissal categories covered in this lesson?
options: Dismissal connected with pregnancy or maternity (s 99)
Dismissal for making a protected disclosure (s 103A)
Dismissal for persistent lateness after several written warnings
Dismissal for asserting a statutory right in good faith (s 104)
testPool.trapExplanation: Persistent lateness after proper warnings is a conduct or capability dismissal assessed under the ordinary unfair dismissal test (Burchell, range of reasonable responses) — it engages none of the automatically unfair categories and, for an employee short of two years' service, may not be actionable at all.

testPool.prompt: Under s 103A ERA 1996, which of these best captures the causal test the tribunal applies?
options: Whether the protected disclosure was the reason, or the principal reason, for the dismissal
Whether any disclosure was made at any point during employment
Whether the employer disputes the disclosure was protected

testPool.prompt: Order the stages a tribunal works through once it has found an automatically unfair dismissal.
items: The tribunal explains reinstatement and re-engagement and asks the claimant's wishes
The tribunal considers whether such an order is practicable
If no order is made, the tribunal proceeds to calculate compensation
The tribunal calculates the basic award and then assesses the compensatory award

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that the basic award compensates the claimant's actual financial loss from dismissal, in the same way the compensatory award does?
sliderLabels: Definitely — same purpose as the compensatory award
Definitely not — a different purpose entirely
testPool.correctPosition: Definitely not — a different purpose entirely
testPool.explanation: The basic award is a formula-based sum tied to age, capped weekly pay and years of service, compensating the fact of dismissal itself — it is calculated the same way as statutory redundancy pay. Actual financial loss is what the separate compensatory award assesses.

testPool.prompt: In the passage below explaining s 124(1A), highlight the sentence that states which categories lose the statutory cap.
testPool.passage: The compensatory award is ordinarily subject to a statutory maximum, set each year and reviewed against 52 weeks' gross pay. Section 124(1A), however, removes that cap for dismissals falling within s 100 (health and safety) or s 103A (protected disclosure). For those two categories, the tribunal assesses compensation purely on the claimant's proven loss, with no statutory ceiling at all.
testPool.ratioSentence: Section 124(1A), however, removes that cap for dismissals falling within s 100 (health and safety) or s 103A (protected disclosure).

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that identifies which automatically unfair category applies on these facts.
testPool.scenarioText: Tomasz has worked for his employer for six weeks. He is dismissed shortly after telling his manager, correctly, that he is entitled to statutory paternity leave and intends to take it. The employer offers no other explanation for the dismissal.
tappableSpans: worked for his employer for six weeks
telling his manager, correctly, that he is entitled to statutory paternity leave
testPool.correctSpan: telling his manager, correctly, that he is entitled to statutory paternity leave
testPool.explanation: This is a family-leave dismissal within s 99 ERA 1996 — asserting his entitlement to paternity leave is the protected act, and his six weeks' service is irrelevant because s 99 requires no qualifying period.

testPool.prompt: An employee dismissed for trade union activities wins her claim and wants her old job back rather than compensation. What must the tribunal do first?
options: Explain reinstatement and re-engagement to her and ask whether she wants such an order, before moving to any question of compensation
Calculate the basic award immediately, since compensation is always assessed before reinstatement is considered
Refuse reinstatement automatically, since it is never available for TULRCA-based dismissals
testPool.explanation: Reinstatement and re-engagement are considered first under s 112(2), for any category of unfair dismissal including TULRCA s 152 claims — compensation is the fallback once that stage is complete or an order proves impracticable.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is most likely to fall within s 104 ERA 1996 (asserting a statutory right), rather than s 103A (whistleblowing)?
testPool.scenarioA: An employee formally requests, in writing, the itemised pay statement she is legally entitled to under s 8 ERA 1996, and is dismissed two days later with no other reason given.
testPool.scenarioB: An employee reports to senior management that a colleague is falsifying safety inspection records, and is dismissed shortly afterwards.
testPool.explanation: A is a s 104 case — the employee is asserting her own statutory entitlement. B is a s 103A case — reporting a colleague's wrongdoing to the employer is a protected disclosure about a matter she is not personally claiming an entitlement to, engaging the whistleblowing provision instead.

testPool.prompt: Fatima has worked for her employer for eight months. She discloses to her line manager, in good faith and with reasonable grounds to believe it, that the company is falsifying environmental compliance records — a matter she reasonably believes is in the public interest. Three weeks later she is dismissed; the employer says only that 'it isn't working out'. She wants both her job back and full compensation for her loss, which exceeds the usual statutory cap. Analyse her position.
factsToOrder: She makes a disclosure in good faith, with reasonable grounds, reasonably believed to be in the public interest
She is dismissed three weeks later with only a vague explanation
Her assessed loss exceeds the usual statutory cap
She wants reinstatement considered as well as compensation

scaffolds.support: Full model answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes the Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, and writes the Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes the full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Fatima's dismissal is automatically unfair under s 103A, what remedy sequence the tribunal follows, and whether the statutory cap limits her compensatory award.
modelAnswer.rule: Section 103A ERA 1996 makes a dismissal automatically unfair, with no qualifying period, where a protected disclosure is the reason or principal reason for dismissal. Remedies proceed under ss 112–124: reinstatement/re-engagement is considered first, then the basic and compensatory awards; s 124(1A) disapplies the statutory cap on the compensatory award for s 103A dismissals.
modelAnswer.application: Fatima's eight months' service is irrelevant, since s 103A requires no qualifying period. Her disclosure appears to meet the qualifying disclosure criteria (reasonable belief, public interest), and the timing plus the employer's vague, unparticularised explanation supports an inference that the disclosure was the principal reason for dismissal. The tribunal must first ask whether she wants reinstatement and assess its practicability before turning to compensation; because this is a s 103A dismissal, the usual statutory cap on the compensatory award does not apply, so she can recover her full assessed loss.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Fatima has a strong automatically unfair dismissal claim under s 103A. The tribunal will consider reinstatement first, and if compensation follows instead, the compensatory award is uncapped.

testPool.prompt: An employee dismissed for a health and safety reason under s 100 ERA 1996 has an assessed loss well above the usual statutory cap. Which statement is correct?
options: The compensatory award is capped at the usual statutory maximum, since s 100 is not one of the listed exceptions
The compensatory award is uncapped, because s 124(1A) disapplies the cap for s 100 dismissals as well as s 103A dismissals
No compensatory award is available at all for s 100 dismissals, only the basic award
testPool.trapExplanation: Students often remember the whistleblowing exception but forget that s 124(1A) disapplies the cap for health and safety dismissals (s 100) too — both categories, not just s 103A, escape the statutory ceiling.

testPool.prompt: An employee with eighteen months' service is dismissed for conduct unrelated to any protected category, and simply falls short of the two-year threshold. How confident are you that she can still bring an ordinary unfair dismissal claim?
testPool.explanation: With no automatically unfair category engaged, the ordinary two-year qualifying period in s 108 applies in full. Eighteen months falls short, so the ordinary unfair dismissal route is closed to her — this is exactly the gap the automatically unfair categories exist to bypass, and exactly why spotting which category (if any) applies matters so much.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The two recurring mistakes in this lesson's test items are treating the two-year qualifying period as universal (it isn't, for the listed categories) and applying the statutory cap mechanically (it's disapplied for s 100 and s 103A dismissals). Both mistakes come from stopping at the headline rule instead of checking whether an exception is in play.
